Zamosc Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zamość, Poland

Demolished. Zamość's Jewish community, present from the 16th century, included both Sephardic and Ashkenazi congregations by the 17th century — a notable dual tradition distinct from the largely Ashkenazi character of most communities documented in this collection. The city produced several figures of major historical significance: Izrael Segal ben Mosze, a Talmudist, pioneer of the Haskalah, and astronomer; Icchak Lejb Perec (I.L. Peretz), one of the three foundational writers of modern Yiddish literature; and Rosa Luxemburg, the internationally significant Marxist theorist and revolutionary, co-founder of Germany's Spartacist League and Communist Party, murdered in 1919. During WWII, a transit ghetto operated in Zamość, and almost everyone held there was murdered at Bełżec or Sobibór in 1942; about 200 Jews returned after the war, but most soon left again. This cemetery was established under a privilege granted in 1588 by Jan Zamoyski, the city's own founder, and grew to 2.80 hectares by 1924 before its closure in 1907. Partially destroyed by German forces during WWII, it suffered further damage from Soviet Army soldiers stationed there in the autumn of 1945; the city built a playground on the site in 1946, followed by a District Telecommunication Office in the 1950s-60s and a District Centre of Culture between 1961 and 1965. No above-ground traces remain today, and there is no form of commemoration.
